# Tales of Tibia — 469, Part 4: "Widespread Madness"

- **URL:** https://article.talesoftibia.com/469/4
- **Retrieved:** 2026-09-04
- **Author:** "Simula" / s2ward

## Archiving note

Structured reconstruction, not a verbatim mirror (see part 1 file). Part 4 is the longest part and is
almost entirely lore synthesis; it contains **no numeric or cryptographic work on 469**, but it does
contain the article's one genuinely methodological contribution to language analysis, recorded below.

## Structure and argument

**§ The Shattered Isles catastrophe.** Three independent NPC accounts are assembled. Malunga: the
isles hold traces of a great civilisation wiped out by a disaster; magic is unevenly distributed, and
where it flows strongly "the savants build magical centres of great importance"; the currents "must
have been more structured once and much stronger than today"; the disaster was at least some
centuries ago and the isles were once a single landmass. Chondur: two powerful races annihilated each
other in a war over the strong magic; the peaceful dwellers were attacked by "a dark power from the
depths of the ocean"; the war "changed the flow of magic forever". Ocelus gives a third variant: two
ancient races, one on land, one in the deep sea.

The author reads the "magical centres of great importance" line as direct in-game confirmation of his
magic-web gate model. He notes parallel geological hints: Roshamuul resembling a piece of the Daraman
continent, and Issavi and Krailos separated by "the great scar".

**§ The Quara as products, not principals.** Chondur says the quara "rose from slavery to a shadow of
their former masters" and served the annihilated dark power. Mermaid NPCs Marina and Maritima are
cited (part-humanoid, part-fish; Maritima says the quara treat fish badly). The author concludes the
quara are amalgamations, i.e. products of dream-shaping, and introduces the term **"the others"** for
the outcast mixed-race faction, rather than naming any one species.

**§ Rathleton / Oramond.** Quotes Oramond folklore research: an ancient race with "technological
knowledge beyond what I've seen anywhere", possibly the mythical Yalahar; when the first humans
arrived the city was already long abandoned; their digging awakened an entity "drawn to sacrifices,
and especially blood", beginning generations of slavery and blood-taxes, ended by the arrival of
'princess' Ramora, for whom no archive holds any record of nobility, dated to the last days of the
Corpse Wars, "in the time when 'dead men walked'". The seapeople are a consistent element across
versions of the exodus and are described as "tall, slender, with pointy ears and bluish skin" —
which the author cross-references to Malunga's line that the extinct civilisation was "possibly of
elven heritage". Glooth is described as slime enhanced with elements, mostly energy.

**§ Fiehonja and the Deepling language (Jekhr).** This is the methodologically interesting section.
The author works from the in-game dictionaries written by **Lagatos**, the Yalaharian chronicler, and
the stated grammar rules: mostly nouns and basic infinite verbs; a written (latin) form used with
NPCs alongside a spoken form; 'T' pronounced "aa" except word-initially where it is 'h'; complex
words built from smaller ones (e.g. `gouthn` "surface" = `gou` "over" + `thn` "face"); a final 'i'
pronounced "ee"; verbs negated by a following `ro`.

He reproduces the article's worked character/transcription/pronunciation/translation tables for
several Deepling books, including a visitor-welcome text and a chant, and notes a deliberate CipSoft
trap: a book that reads as a benign message ("who do you believe? Kjell! Kjell brings light") is
revealed by cross-referencing the dictionary to be about **obedience** — `kohn` derives from
`roqohn`, non-believer/non-obeyer.

He then takes on the two **SENX** books, which he says "cannot be found anywhere online and can
barely be translated using the provided dictionaries". His method: the language has **evolved**, so
consonants have shifted between the older and younger tongues. He derives the correspondences by
matching near-identical words across the two corpora:

```
TO = ho        DONSAXT = donsakh    JARXT = jarkh    FLAT = flah
JUVN = jubn    UWTE = umte          XOLX = kolk      LOUDJOT = loudjou
JTLI = jhli    XWEIJ = kweij        WOT = moh        VOLWOT = bolmoh
ARJAX = arjak
```

yielding the substitution rules **T→H, X→K, W→M, V→B** (and, in the second book, H→T). Applying them
produces readable text about Senx, an "invader of the deep" who heralds the second coming.

This is a real, checkable, internally-consistent piece of philological work and is the only part of
the whole series that resembles cryptanalysis.

**§ The Navigator.** The article's best-supported in-game deduction. The Navigator claims to have
been captain of the Skyflare, saved by a strange fish-ornamented armour whose trader spoke of a
"blessed breath" and "to subdue the drift", and to have been mistaken by the Njey for their god-king
Qjell: "I practically rewrote their history. I WAS THE SECOND COMING." He says he controls everything
from his room through funnels that carry his voice, that the stones on the beach and the trader were
all him, and that he has been navigating the fate of the land for more than a century.

The author's tells that the Navigator is lying about his origin: he was a captain but calls himself
the Navigator; claims Thais origin yet has an ornamented carpet and a house of Deepling steel; has a
"469 machine" and steelwork made only by Yalaharian golems; has a shimmer glower, which requires
Deepling eyes; and **responds to the keyword LAGATOS**. He concludes Navigator = Lagatos, and
probably also = Faltugios, and that *The Swimmer* books (the only Jekhr texts with no second edition)
are Lagatos's own account of himself.

**§ Yalahar and Variphor.** Quotes the Yalahar plaques: the Yalahari were among the most advanced
races of the god wars, their flaw being intelligence; their mago-scientists detected a "missing
factor" in all world-views and calculations; they established an "approximation theory" of a place
between reality and non-reality inhabited by an entity they named **Variphor** — and by naming it,
gave it substance. Most of the race destroyed each other in a night of slaughter; the remainder left
the world. The Hive books (the paranoid captain's eight-book diary about "IT", the killing of
Faltugios and Traks, the ghost visitations, the destroyed outbound ship, and the captain's final
self-deification and death) are quoted at length as the practical illustration.

The author's synthesis: the Yalahari created the **Lightbearers** to fight Variphor and spread light,
built towers of importance across Tibia, and after the catastrophe fled — some to Beregar, becoming
dwarves who later moved to Kazordoon. Supporting details offered: Lokur's poem in Beregar about two
tribes united in the land of the gods who fought and split; Pythius the Rotten's claim to have
watched Yalahar's research and taken their treasures after they slaughtered themselves; Emperor Rehal
mentioning a dwarf "rather tall for our kind"; Rehon son of Rehal versus the Hive's Rehus; the elven
naming convention "son/daughter of ___"; and Uzgod being the only known smith of ancient steel.

**§ The one-language hypothesis.** The author asks why Tibia has roughly seven constructed languages
and proposes there may be only one, evolved. Method reported honestly, including the negative result:
he transposed the Ankrahmun chant, checked which words fell within one character of dictionary
entries (`orum ~ grum` enemies / `krum` will; `taa ~ taan` face; `moaa` ground; `da'aa ~ daa` to;
`dojaa ~ doaa` wipe; `meaa` bed, `meaarem` sleep/dream), then transposed a Deepling English book and
concluded: **"Structure is not at all similar. The books of SENX are not at all similar."** and "Sure,
we can skew it for our theory and make it better. But we need something more."

He reports collecting every Tibian language from Ugha to Chakoya, transposing them and running
**character frequency analysis**, finding "similarities in the top 7 characters", and that unrelated
real languages (Finnish, French, English) were not nearly as close to each other after the same
treatment. He then explicitly discounts his own method: "knowing that the language has evolved with
time, made frequency analysis not as useful."

His best positive evidence is a lexical triple: Lazaran the caveman explains that his friend **Tatak**
was named for war drums ("He sound our war drums! That were name come from. Tanakk! Tanakk!"), while
in Jekhr `nakk` = weapon and `tanakk` = armed; and in Jekhr X = KS in the current tongue and K in the
older, giving `naxx`/`tanaxx` — with **Jaccus Maxxen** offered as a third instance. He also notes the
excess of 'a' across Djinn names, Pharaoh names and caveman names.

His resolution of the elves-versus-humans ordering is the same Mad Mage book quoted in part 1: "I
watched the first elves struggling to form a nation with the help of the lightbearers" — placing the
lightbearers, and therefore humans, before the elves. He connects "QJELL BRINGER LIGHT" to
"LIGHTBEARER BRINGER LIGHT".

Crucially, he concedes the design intent: the shared-language conceit "is also a great plot device for
the content creators, as they likely didn't intend for the language to be completely translatable.
It's a way for them to still make it understandable and 'solveable', while still giving us the reason
why it can't be translated. **It was never intended to.**"
